title: Nandy 'minded to intervene' in Sky's £1.6bn takeover of ITV entertainment arm
content: Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has said she is "minded to intervene" in the proposed £1.6bn deal for Sky to buy ITV's media and entertainment division. Nandy said there were reasonable grounds to believe the deal could affect free expression in the media and the variety of Britain's news landscape. Sky said it would "carefully consider" a letter from the culture secretary and "engage constructively" with the review into the deal. "We remain confident that bringing Sky and ITV's media and entertainment business together will create a stronger British media," it said. ITV welcomed the letter and said the deal would help it "compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries". The two companies announced in July that Sky had agreed to buy ITV's broadcasting business, including its free-to-air TV channels and the ITV X streaming service. The deal does not include ITV's production arm, ITV Studios, which makes popular programmes such as Love Island and I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here. It would give Sky access to millions more viewers, while bosses hope it would help both compete with streaming giants such as Netflix. But Nandy has told Sky and ITV that she is considering issuing a public interest intervention notice (PIIN) to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) and regulator Ofcom, forcing an investigation into the tie-up. In a letter to both companies, she said she was minded to order the probe to address public interest considerations including: The letter said Nandy recognised Sky News and ITV News were two of the most prominent sources of television news in the UK, with a joint 26% share of those viewing news on linear TV. Consumers would still have access to other sources of news such as the BBC and Channel 4, it added. But Nandy believes that, over time, the tie-up could undermine the range of views available to viewers, with 86% of the linear TV news market controlled by the BBC and Sky/ITV. The North of England could be particularly hard hit as well as nations of the UK other than England and those from lower socio-economic backgrounds, the letter argued. This is because their main source of news is broadcast news, it added. Sky and ITV have been given until 20 October to respond to the culture secretary's concerns. A Sky spokesperson said: "We have already made clear commitments to protect ITV's identity, its free-to-air services and public service broadcasting obligations, and to ensure ITV News and Sky News remain distinct editorial voices." An ITV spokesperson said: "We welcome the publication of the secretary of state's 'minded to' issue a public interest intervention notice letter as was expected and look forward to fully co-operating in the process. "This is another important milestone in the regulatory review process towards creating a UK player with the scale and resources to better compete with global streaming platforms, benefiting viewers, advertisers and the UK creative industries." Nandy's intervention would be made under a new public interest consideration. This would need legislation to be brought forward, given that current laws do not cover the effect of a merger on streaming or on-demand programmes. She said: "If I decide to intervene on the basis of this new public interest consideration, I will bring forward legislation... to extend the application of the public interest consideration relating to the availability of a wide range of broadcasting to on-demand programmes." title: Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget
content: The UK economy's stronger than expected performance in August has been called a "sign of resilience" by Chancellor John Healey. Healey told the BBC "it's really tough in the face of these economic global shocks" as the latest official figures showed the economy grew by 0.1% for the month, defying analysts' forecasts of a slight contraction. It follows an upgrade to this year's forecast for the UK economy from global watchdog the International Monetary Fund (IMF) earlier this week. Mr Healey said he wanted "to give people a bit of breathing space from the cost of living and cost of business pressures", promising to do so when he delivers his first Budget in two weeks' time. Healey did not elaborate on what measures he will take in the Budget, but promised "where we can take action, we will". But, vowing to keep up the government's approach to fiscal discipline, Healey said "where we want to do things we have to make sure we can pay for them within the Budget that we've got and control spending". The latest figures from the Office for National Statistics showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to August. "It's a sign of resilience in the UK economy that some had not expected," Healey said. The chancellor said the growth was "part of the discipline the IMF here in Bangkok this week has endorsed that they see in Britain". Britain's economy was boosted in August by an increase in production, which includes manufacturing, oil and gas extraction and energy supply. The services industry, which makes up the largest chunk of the UK's economy, was flat during the month, while the construction sector contracted. Over the three months to August, the UK's economy grew by 0.7% overall. ONS director of economic statistics Liz McKeown said computer programming had been the biggest contributor to what she described as "robust" growth over the period. But she said the production and construction sectors shrank over the three-month period. August's surprise expansion follows growth of 0.4% in July. The ONS also upgraded its estimate for June's monthly growth to 0.4% from 0.3%. Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said Britain's economy was "more robust than we thought". He warned that an expected increase in inflation would still "dampen growth", but added that the economy was showing "remarkable resilience to higher energy prices and borrowing costs". PwC senior economist Jake Finney said the development of AI infrastructure was underpinning Britain's relatively strong performance. "The UK still lags the US in both the scale of that investment and the boost it provides to growth, but it is making progress and remains ahead of many of its European peers," he added. Healey told the BBC the "impact of AI on the economy, on productivity, is only just beginning to register". He said the technology has "huge potential, as well as huge risks", adding that Britain's priority would be to ensure AI can be developed safely while unlocking the opportunities it presents. The latest growth figures were released after Healey landed in Bangkok for the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Earlier this week, the global financial watchdog praised the UK's plans to cut debt levels, with global borrowing costs on the rise, with managing director Kristalina Georgieva adding that the country was seeing "a bit of a better growth prospect" than other G7 nations. Healey said: "Despite conflicts in the Middle East and Europe hitting people across the world, today's figures offer more proof of Britain's resilience in the face of these global shocks." The Conservatives said the economic growth figures "conceal worrying trends in key sectors as we approach a crucial Budget". Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Construction has now shrunk for four months in a row, with private housebuilding falling fastest. Labour promised to get Britain building, but they are failing." He called for Healey to cut taxes and reduce red tape. Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, Daisy Cooper, said the growth of 0.1% in August was "nothing to celebrate". "The economy is stuck in first gear and barely crawling forward, while families are still struggling to make ends meet." Healey went on to say the Budget would be tough and not include inflation top-ups for public sector pay. Some experts and unions have called for extra cash for some departmental budgets, to account for the rising costs of providing public services and pay. But, asked whether there would be extra money made available for nurses and doctors, the chancellor said: "People recognise these times that are tough for everyone, and what they do expect of a government is to manage with the budgets we've got, deliver the public services they need, and that's the challenge. "Our departments have their spending, and the prime minister and I, being in lockstep about this, where we want to do things, we have to make sure that we can pay for them within the budgets that we've got and control spending."
